Costa Rica’s Chemicals Sector Disrupted by Nationwide Worker Walkout

SAN JOSÉ — The chemicals industry in Costa Rica was brought to a near-standstill on Monday as thousands of workers staged a coordinated walkout demanding improved wages and working conditions, according to union representatives and industry sources. The strike, which began in the early hours, has already led to significant disruptions in production and delivery across the country, affecting both domestic and export operations.

Empaques Universal SA, one of the leading manufacturers of industrial packaging materials, confirmed that its main facility in Cartago was operating at minimal capacity due to the absence of most of its production staff. “We are facing critical delays in fulfilling client orders, and our logistics chain is under strain,” said Laura Jiménez, operations manager at Empaques Universal SA. “We urge all parties to find a swift resolution to minimize further economic impact.”

The National Union of Chemical Workers (Sindicato Nacional de Trabajadores Químicos) stated that around 3,500 employees from over 20 companies joined the walkout, citing stagnant wages amid rising living costs and concerns over occupational safety. “Our members have been negotiating for months without meaningful progress,” said union leader Marco Ureña. “Today’s action is a last resort, not just for higher pay, but for safer working conditions.”

According to the Costa Rican Chamber of Chemical Industries, the sector had already been facing pressures from international competition and fluctuating raw material prices. “This walkout compounds existing challenges,” said Ana María Rojas, spokesperson for the chamber. “Several companies are reporting daily financial losses in the range of $100,000 to $250,000, depending on their scale and export commitments.”

At Empaques Universal SA, management reported that only about 15% of its workforce was present on Monday, resulting in the temporary suspension of two of its three production lines. “Every hour of lost production puts our international contracts at risk,” Jiménez said. “We are maintaining open communication with clients, but the situation remains highly uncertain.”

Union representatives indicated that the strike would continue until employers and government officials return to negotiations with “concrete proposals.” Analysts said the chemicals industry, which contributed over $1.1 billion to Costa Rica’s GDP last year, stands to see significant impacts if the dispute is not resolved promptly.

Government mediators have called for urgent talks, but as of Monday evening, both sides remained at a stalemate and the walkout showed no sign of abating.
